core: working definition of planning, attributed to OpenStax Principles of Management (17.1): planning is the process by which managers establish goals and specify how these goals are to be attained — setting objectives and deciding the course of action to achieve them
the two components of a plan: outcome or goal statements (the end state) and action statements (the means)

why organizations plan, grouped as direction (focusing activity on objectives), coordination (a systematic road map), and efficient use of resources (economic efficiency), with OpenStax's five reasons as the underlying evidence
the plan types named: strategic, tactical, and operational, each with a one-line description and an original example (Cascade Coffee)
the planning process in four steps: assess the situation, set objectives, choose actions, monitor — distilled from the Koontz-O'Donnell model as presented by OpenStax (17.2)
plans versus goals: the destination versus the route; goal-setting is a sibling topic, referenced only
planning and uncertainty: plans rest on premises and change when conditions change (OpenStax 17.1/17.2; CFI)
the honest framing: a plan is a hypothesis about the future — a reasoned guess tested against reality, not a promise
supporting: OpenStax's full five-reason list for planning: offset uncertainty and change; focus organizational activity on objectives; provide a coordinated, systematic road map; increase economic efficiency; facilitate control by establishing a standard (17.1)

the full five-step planning model (awareness of the present state, establishing outcome statements, premising, determining a course of action, formulating supportive plans) and the Deming cycle of plan-do-check-act (17.2)
contingency plans as alternative courses of action for when planning assumptions prove wrong (17.3)

CFI's six-step strategic planning process: define mission and objectives, formulate strategy (situation assessment such as SWOT), implement, translate into actionable plans, evaluate, review and adjust; strategic plans must evolve as conditions change
managers use conversation to gather information and develop plans (OpenStax POM 1.1); top managers spend more time on long-range planning than first-line managers (OpenStax POM 1.3)
outOfScope: goal-setting — sibling topic owns how to write good objectives (SMART etc.); this lesson treats goals only as the input planning turns into action
decision-making — sibling topic owns how managers choose among alternatives in depth; this lesson names 'choose actions' as one planning step only
controlling — sibling topic owns the control function; monitoring appears here only as the planning checkpoint that feeds back into the plan
organizing and leading — sibling topics own the other management functions
management-by-objectives, budgets as single-use plans, forecasting techniques, and planning software — practitioner detail outside this lesson
strategic-management depth (SWOT mechanics, competitive strategy frameworks, mission-writing) — referenced only as part of the strategic-plan type

claims.claim: Planning is the process by which managers establish goals and specify how these goals are to be attained; OpenStax's Principles of Management frames planning as the function of deciding objectives and the course of action to achieve them, and this lesson attributes the working definition to OpenStax.

Plans have two basic components: outcome or goal statements, which represent the end state — the targets and outcomes managers hope to attain — and action statements, which reflect the means by which organizations move forward to attain their goals.

Managers plan to offset uncertainty and change, to focus organizational activity on a set of objectives, to provide a coordinated and systematic road map for future activities, to increase economic efficiency, and to facilitate control by establishing a standard for later activity; this lesson groups these as direction, coordination, and resource use.

The planning process, adapted from Koontz and O'Donnell as presented by OpenStax, includes developing an awareness of the present state, establishing outcome statements, premising (setting assumptions), determining a course of action with action statements, and formulating supportive plans; plans must then be monitored, and planning links to controlling and to the Deming cycle of plan, do, check, act.

Strategic plans address the organization's institutional level and outline a long-term vision, often anchored in the mission; tactical plans are division-level or unit-level plans designed to help the organization accomplish its strategic plans; operating plans provide direction and action statements for activities in the organization's technical core; contingency plans are alternative courses of action for when planning assumptions prove wrong.

Strategic planning is creating specific business strategies, implementing them, and evaluating the results against the company's long-term goals; the process includes defining mission and objectives, formulating strategy after assessing the situation (e.g., SWOT), implementing, translating strategy into actionable plans with assigned responsibilities and timelines, evaluating performance, and reviewing and adjusting — strategic plans must evolve as conditions change.

The quality and success of any plan depends on the quality of its underlying premises or assumptions, and planning should be an ongoing process in which plans are continually monitored and modified to accommodate changing conditions and new information.

Managers spend most of their working time with other people and use conversation to gather information, identify problems, and develop plans; top managers' activity mix is heavier on long-range planning and coordination than that of first-line managers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many steps the planning process has
positions: OpenStax (following Koontz and O'Donnell) presents a five-step model: awareness, outcome statements, premising, course of action, supportive plans.
CFI presents a six-step strategic planning process: mission and objectives, formulation, implementation, actionable plans, evaluation, review and adjust.

This lesson uses a four-step simplification — assess the situation, set objectives, choose actions, monitor — that keeps the spine of the OpenStax model (steps 1, 2, and 4 plus the monitoring requirement) while staying at general literacy level.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No substantive conflict: all sources agree planning starts from the current situation, sets objectives, chooses actions, and revisits the plan. The step counts differ by granularity, and the lesson presents the four-step version explicitly as a distillation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'planning' and 'plans' are the same thing
positions: Some business writing uses 'planning' for the function and 'plans' for the documents it produces.
OpenStax uses planning for the ongoing process and plans for their two components (outcome and action statements).
This lesson follows OpenStax: planning is the process; a plan is its output, with a destination part and a route part.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Terminological, not substantive; the lesson states the distinction explicitly.

rightsIssues: OpenStax Principles of Management is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and its page footer states the book may not be ingested into LLMs without OpenStax's permission; all OpenStax-derived content in this lesson is therefore paraphrased into original prose (reference-only usage), with only the one-sentence working definition quoted with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 17.2: The Planning Process
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20251109184247/ on 2026-08-22. Supports the Koontz-O'Donnell planning model: developing an awareness of the present state; establishing outcome statements; premising (assumptions about the future, surfaced, monitored, updated); determining a course of action with action statements (what, when, how, by whom); formulating supportive plans; planning feeding controlling by establishing standards; the Deming cycle (plan, do, check, act). The lesson's four-step framing (assess, set objectives, choose actions, monitor) is a distillation of this model, stated as such.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 17.3: Types of Plans
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20250430110756/ on 2026-08-22. Supports: strategic plans address the organization's institutional level, outline a long-term vision, and are anchored in the mission; tactical plans as division-level or unit-level plans designed to help the organization accomplish its strategic plans; operating plans providing direction and action statements for the technical core; contingency plans as alternative courses of action for when planning assumptions prove wrong; the further a plan projects into the future, the more uncertainty planners encounter. All facts restated in original prose.
